title: The Blood of Dawnwalker - best settings to tweak
summary: The recommended specs are a little over-generous so here are the settings I reckon you can compromise to gain some extra performance.
body: The Blood of Dawnwalker is a punishing game. And not just because of the divisive time-as-a-resource-to-be-managed side of things (or the almost impossible to resist desire to shift 'the' around in the title) but because it will slay your PC in terms of performance. We've covered the fact that in order to hit any of the performance level system requirements you have to enable upscaling in Balanced mode , but it's also worth noting that those system requirements are a little generous, too. I've been testing Dawnwalker for the past week or so, with a few different setups, and in those forests of Carpathia you're going to either need some more beefy hardware to hit Rebel Wolves' proposed frame rate targets or compromise on those graphics settings. Which is where I'm coming in here, aiming to help you get the highest frame rate out of your rig without sacrificing the actual look of the game. And, actually The Blood of Dawnwalker does pretty well even down at the lower end of the graphics settings, still looking relatively crisp and with a detailed open world for you to explore to your vampyric heart's content. As a representative system, I've picked out Rebel Wolves' mid-range spec, t…

title: Dwarf Fortress co-creator says his life as a millionaire is 'basically like reattaining what my parents could do with regular jobs'
summary: Tarn Adams lives in a house now. I bet that's nice.
body: Back in 2024, Dwarf Fortress surpassed 800,000 copies sold, more than enough to make co-creators Tarn and Zach Adams millionaires . At the time, they seemed to be taking a low-key approach to the whole mo' money thing, so when our intrepid interviewer Joshua Wolens caught up with Tarn at the recently-concluded Gamescom, he asked if, in the two years since then, he'd more fully adjusted to his moneybags lifestyle. "I guess, a bit, somewhat. I mean, I live in a house now. I have two cats and they love me. That's great," Adams said. But, he added, it wasn't so much a matter of adjusting to something new as just going back to what used to be. "I know what [having a house] is like because I grew up in one. It's basically like reattaining what my parents could do with regular jobs. It's not much different from that. "And I don't want to make light of financial security, right? I mean, yeah, that's great, and I wish it for everybody." It makes me think of Adams' comments in the same interview about enabling a more equitable, better-functioning society in Dwarf Fortress by walling up dwarf nobles and abolishing the dwarf cops: He said there's perhaps a " lesson to be had there ." title: OpenAI head Sam Altman says 'people hate data centers,' but the company still plans to invest $50 million more in AI infrastructure this year alone
summary: Putting two and two together, but coming up with a completely different answer.
body: Earlier this year, shots were fired and an incendiary device was thrown at the house of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. In a recent interview with Time , he reflected on the past year: "It has been a painful personal experience. Clearly, people hate data centres—right now, at least. People are pretty negative on AI." Does that mean OpenAI is packing it in, and going home? Well, no. The AI infrastructure buildout is continuing in earnest, with OpenAI planning to invest another $50 million this year alone on collecting compute. Sachin Katti, the co-lead on OpenAI's compute strategy told Time that the company's earlier investments now appear "very prescient," going on to add, "We are still short of compute. If anything, we should have bought a lot more." If OpenAI's machine-learning products don't bring in the revenue the company would like, renting out its compute capacity to other parties is another option. Altman told Time, "I think we are going to be able to use all of the compute very profitably that we are planning to build." Intent on investing millions more either way, it makes me wonder where the company will find the space to build—not just in terms of logistics, but also in terms o…

title: Resident Evil 2's director believes Capcom has become 'completely numb to how scary' recent games have been and wants a 'non-horror mode'
summary: Ok, so, the zombies don't want to eat you, they just want a hug—wait, that's still scary.
body: Something's wrong with me. No matter how many horror games I play, I just can't get scared like I used to. Perhaps I'm the problem—maybe a decade of playing horror games pretty much non-stop has irrevocably altered my brain chemistry. Take Resident Evil Requiem , for example—that just doesn't make the cut for a horror game in my book. Apart from the first five minutes in the underground cells, there just wasn't anything that felt particularly scary. In fact, I don't believe that any horror game that gives me a gun can be scary, except for Amnesia: The Bunker—I genuinely thought that game was going to kill me. Again, I find myself thinking that there's something up with my nervous system, because even Hideki Kamiya, director of Resident Evil 2 , would disagree with me. He believes that Capcom has become blind to just how scary its recent games have become. "I've never been a fan of horror. I mean, even from the time I was young, I could never handle it," Kamiya says in an interview with VGC . "I don’t like horror, and I don’t like scary things. title: Former id Software producer says the team faced the 'worst crunch' in the series' history on Doom: The Dark Ages – Revelations: 'There were days where I didn't see my son'
summary: "There were two months where I was working something like at least 12 hours every day."
body: The situation surrounding Doom: The Dark Ages – Revelations was already grim. Id Software put out a fantastic expansion that addressed many issues present in the ( still pretty good ) base game, placing it among the best works the FPS specialists have ever produced. The reward for many of The Dark Ages team was to be instantly laid off , as Xbox cut 136 members of the studio's workforce. Now, it also appears that getting Revelations to the finish line was a punishing experience for those involved, at least according to former id Software producer Andrew Willis. Speaking on the Kiwi Talkz podcast for Insider Gaming , Willis revealed that the team experienced a gnarly level of crunch in the months leading up to Revelations' release. "It was tight," Willis explained. "There were two months where I was working something like at least 12 hours every day. I know I hit 17 a couple of days." Willis goes on to describe the experience as "brutal" and says that most of the expansion was put together "in three or four months." That's a ridiculously short turnaround for an expansion that's around six hours long, especially when you consider the main game—which runs at about 20 hours—took five …
